description: Team Pathfinder is Kartik Agarwal, me , a student who loves space and wanted to make Moon mission planning simple enough for anyone to understand. Working solo, I designed, tested and validated the Lunar Landing Site Navigator, using AI as a coding assistant and NASA data as its foundation.
summary:
WHAT IT DOES: Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a free web app that shows whether a site near the Moon's south pole has sunlight for solar power and a view of Earth for direct radio contact, and for how long. Users tap one of NASA's Artemis III candidate regions or drop their own pin, then see the Sun and Earth against the real terrain skyline.

FEATURES: Live horizon view with time-lapse; power and radio timelines up to a year ahead; five key numbers and an explainable 0-100 score; side-by-side site comparison; a best-window finder that ranks every start date at every site for any mission length; a rotatable 3D Moon; a learning mode with guided tour, glossary and classroom worksheet; CSV, PNG, Mission Brief and share-link export.

HOW IT WORKS: Sun and Earth positions come from astronomy-engine with the IAU lunar rotation model. Terrain horizons in 360 directions come from NASA LRO/LOLA elevation data (240 m grid). Everything runs in the browser.

VALIDATION: Checked live against NASA JPL Horizons (within 0.007 degrees) and NASA LOLA illumination maps. All 22 checks pass.

BENEFITS: Fast first look for mission planners, hands-on lessons for teachers, and an easy way for the public to follow Artemis. Free, no login, works on a tablet.

TOOLS: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Three.js, astronomy-engine, GitHub Pages.
details:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a free web app that helps mission planners, teachers and the public compare landing sites near the Moon's south pole in seconds. At the south pole the Sun never climbs more than a degree or two above a smooth horizon, so a single hill can cast a shadow that lasts for days, and the Earth slowly rises and sets because of the Moon's monthly wobble. A lander needs sunlight for its solar panels and a clear view of the Earth to talk to mission control. Tools that calculate this already exist, but they are complicated and slow to use, so we set out to build something anyone could understand in seconds.

You start by choosing a site. The app includes NASA's nine Artemis III candidate regions from the October 2024 list, four reference points from earlier NASA studies, and the option to drop your own pin anywhere between 80 degrees south and the pole. As soon as a site is selected, a horizon view shows the real terrain skyline all the way around it, with the Sun and the Earth drawn in their true positions. Pressing Play runs a time-lapse so you can watch them move across the sky, and the app explains what you are seeing in plain words, for example "Sun is 6.2 degrees above the horizon, solar power available" or "Earth in view, direct radio link possible." It also tells you how long the light or the radio link will last.

To look further ahead, the Timeline view shows coloured strips for power, radio contact and the times when both are available together, for any period from thirty days to a full year. Five key numbers summarise each site: the share of time in sunlight, the longest period of darkness, the share of time the Earth is visible, the longest radio gap, and the overlap of power and radio. These combine into an overall score from 0 to 100, and a breakdown shows exactly why a site earned its score. Users can change the weights to match their own priorities, compare two to four sites side by side, and see a full-year ranking of every site.

The Best Window finder is designed for real planning. You enter a mission length, such as seven, fourteen or thirty days, and the app tests every possible start date at every site, hour by hour, and ranks the results. On the first screen, one-tap questions such as "Best seven-day landing window in 2027" give the answer in a single sentence. Results can be exported as spreadsheets, images, a one-page Mission Brief, or a link that reopens the exact same view.

To make the science easy to explore, a 3D Moon can be rotated and zoomed with a finger, with the Sun's lighting and the Earth's direction following the time slider. A learning mode adds a short guided tour, a glossary where any technical word can be tapped for an explanation, and a printable worksheet for classrooms. Simple and Expert modes let beginners and specialists see the level of detail they need.

Behind the scenes, the app calculates the positions of the Sun and the Earth using astronomy-engine, an open-source library verified against NASA JPL data, together with the International Astronomical Union's lunar rotation model, which accounts for the Moon's wobble. It then compares those positions with a 360-degree horizon for each site, built from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter laser altimeter (LOLA) elevation data on a 240-metre grid. All calculations run in the browser, with heavy work done in the background so the page stays smooth. There is nothing to install, no login, no tracking, and it works on a tablet, even offline after the first visit.

Because accuracy matters, the Validation page runs 22 checks live every time it is opened. Across 110 comparisons, our Sun and Earth positions match NASA JPL Horizons to within 0.007 degrees. Our yearly sunlight figures are within about three percentage points of NASA's LOLA illumination maps on average across twelve sites, and crater floors that NASA maps as permanently shadowed also receive no sunlight in our model. All 22 checks pass. We were also careful to be honest about limits: site positions are approximate, the terrain grid cannot see boulders, and radio visibility does not model antennas or ground stations. Each of these is clearly labelled in the app.

We built the project with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Three.js and astronomy-engine, and host it on GitHub Pages. Claude, an AI model by Anthropic, helped write the code, documentation and demo, while we made the design decisions, tested the tool and checked the results against NASA references. In the future we would like to add finer terrain around each site, relay satellites for far-side communication, the lunar north pole, and eventually other worlds.
